compensating.why: hop 1 also returns type variables unchanged
hop 3 maps a generic array type to its raw array class
hop 4 resolves the type against its own raw type before passing it on

ownership_reason: Only the gold tells the kinds of type apart and gives each kind its canonical implementation; hops 1-4 hold the type only to pass it on (hop 1 also returns null for null) and get back one Type, which cannot be traced back to the branch that produced it. The gold's javadoc promises the type in canonical form (functionally equal, not necessarily equal by Object.equals): the class String[].class and the GenericArrayType of String are functionally equal, and their canonical forms must be equal, because TypeToken equality compares canonical types; on the trigger input the gold returns the array class as a Class while it turns the GenericArrayType built by TypeToken.getArray into Gson's GenericArrayTypeImpl. The convention is pinned outside the gold: $Gson$Types.resolve represents a resolved array class by arrayOf(component), the same array-class-to-GenericArrayType step; TypeToken.getArray makes the GenericArrayType the array form of a TypeToken; $Gson$Types.getArrayComponentType and ArrayTypeAdapter's factory treat an array class and a GenericArrayType alike; GenericArrayTypeTest::testOurTypeFunctionality pins that arrayOf(List<String>) and the canonical type of TypeToken<List<String>[]> are equal with equal hash codes, and TypeTokenTest::testParameterizedFactory pins the same equality for parameterized types. A hop that converts array classes itself (before the gold or instead of it) is a second implementation of the gold's per-kind decision in a method documented as passing the type on; the gold then still returns an array class unchanged, contrary to its own contract.
